civilopediaText.text: Deep water. Only used on randomly generated maps - the invasion beaches lie on the shallow Bay of the Seine.

The Bay of the Seine, the shallow stretch of the Channel off the Normandy coast. On the morning of D-Day a north-west wind of force 4 to 5 raised waves of four to six feet; many men in the landing craft were seasick before they reached the beach.
Allied land units can cross it embarked in landing craft. German units cannot enter it.
Ponds and lakes.

civilopediaText.text: Pasture: the lush, wet meadows of the Bessin and the Cotentin, where Normandy's cattle grazed among the apple trees. Almost every field is walled by hedgerows (see Bocage); the rest is open ground.

civilopediaText.text: Fields: the open, rolling wheat and corn country of the Caen plain, between the Seulles and the Dives. Good going for tanks, with long fields of fire - and nowhere to hide from them.

civilopediaText.text: Hills and high ground - the Caumont ridge, Hill 112 above the Odon. Whoever holds them sees for miles across the bocage.

civilopediaText.text: Gentle ridges - the Périers ridge north of Caen, the Bréville ridge east of the Orne. Easy to cross, but the crest gives a view over the country around it.

name: Forest

civilopediaText.text: Woods: the Forêt de Cerisy, the Bois de Bavent, and woodlots everywhere. They hide troops from view and from the fighter-bombers.

name: Bocage
uniques: Blocks line-of-sight from tiles at same elevation

civilopediaText.text: The bocage: a maze of small fields, each walled by a bank of earth three or four feet high and topped with a thick hedge and trees, with sunken lanes between them. Allied planners had studied the beaches for months but badly underestimated the hedgerows behind them.

Every field was a fortress: a defender with a machine gun covered the gate, and tanks that tried to climb the banks showed their thin belly armour. The Americans called the fighting in it 'hedgerow hell'.
Apple orchards - the cider and Calvados country. Some cover from view, little protection.

name: Town
uniques: Blocks line-of-sight from tiles at same elevation

civilopediaText.text: Stone-built Norman towns and villages. Every house is a strongpoint for a defender; the Allied bombing that smashed many of them often only made better rubble to defend.

Wide, flat sand beaches backed by dunes or a sea wall. At low tide on D-Day the sand stretched hundreds of yards from the waterline to the shingle, studded with steel hedgehogs, wooden stakes and ramps tipped with mines, and swept by machine guns. There is no cover on a beach: -10% defence.

name: Bluffs
uniques: Has an elevation of [1] for visibility calculations

civilopediaText.text: The steep, grassy bluffs, a hundred to a hundred and fifty feet high, that rise behind the shingle of Omaha Beach. German strongpoints along the top looked straight down on the beach. The only ways up for vehicles were five narrow gullies - the 'draws'.

name: Cliffs
uniques: Has an elevation of [1] for visibility calculations

civilopediaText.text: Sheer limestone cliffs, like those from Pointe du Hoc to Vierville and from Port-en-Bessin to Arromanches. Almost impossible to land under or to climb - except for the Rangers.

Rommel had the low meadows behind Utah Beach and along the Douve, the Merderet, the Aure and the Dives flooded. From the air they looked like fields; many paratroopers who came down in them drowned, weighed down by their equipment. The only ways across were narrow causeways - the roads.
Rivers and canals - the Douve, the Merderet, the Vire, the Aure, the Seulles, the Orne and the Caen Canal, the Dives. They run along tile edges.
Crossing a river away from a bridge takes all remaining movement, and attacking across one costs -20%. Roads have bridges - which is why the airborne divisions were sent to seize them.

Strongpoint WN 5 at La Madeleine, held by a company of the 919th Grenadier Regiment under 23-year-old Leutnant Arthur Jahnke, guarding Exit 2 - the causeway across the flooded fields behind Utah Beach.
The current carried the first wave a mile south of its target, onto a stretch the bombers had smashed. Utah Beach cost the 4th Division fewer than 200 casualties - the lightest of all five beaches.
KEY POSITION: in the D-Day scenario a city stands here at the start of the battle. At nightfall on June 8 the Allies win if they hold at least 10 of the 13 key positions; otherwise Germany wins.

name: Sainte-Mere-Eglise
uniques: Blocks line-of-sight from tiles at same elevation

civilopediaText.text: The little market town on the Cherbourg highway. A house fire had woken the townspeople and the German garrison when the first paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne came down into the square; Private John Steele hung from the church steeple for two hours, feigning death.

At 4:30 AM the 505th Parachute Infantry took the town and raised the American flag over the town hall - the first town in France liberated by the Americans. The Germans counterattacked it from north and south all day and into June 7.

civilopediaText.text: The town at the base of the Cotentin, where the highway from Cherbourg crosses the Douve marshes on a long causeway - 'Purple Heart Lane' to the 101st Airborne. Von der Heydte's paratroopers held it until June 12.
Until Carentan fell, the Utah and Omaha beachheads could not join up.

civilopediaText.text: A promontory of hundred-foot cliffs between Utah and Omaha, with a battery of six 155mm guns in open pits and casemates that could fire on both beaches.

At 7:10 AM, 225 men of the 2nd Ranger Battalion under Lt. Col. James Rudder fired grapnels to the top and climbed under fire. They found the gun positions empty: the guns had been moved inland, where a Ranger patrol found and destroyed them in an orchard. The Rangers then held the point for two days against counterattacks.

civilopediaText.text: The Les Moulins draw at Saint-Laurent-sur-Mer, one of the five gullies leading up the bluffs off Omaha Beach, guarded by strongpoints WN 66 and WN 68.

On Omaha the bombers had missed, the DD tanks had sunk and the 352nd Division was waiting. By mid-morning Bradley thought of abandoning the beach - but small groups led by officers and NCOs were already working their way up the bluffs between the strongpoints. Omaha cost about 2,400 American casualties on D-Day.

civilopediaText.text: The fishing harbour between Omaha and Gold, overlooked by cliffs and strongpoints on both sides. 47 Royal Marine Commando, landing on Gold, marched ten miles west behind the German lines and took it on the night of June 7-8 - linking the British and American beachheads. It later became the terminal of the PLUTO fuel pipeline.

civilopediaText.text: The fortified seafront village at the western end of Gold Beach. A 75mm gun in a casemate at WN 37, shielded from the sea and firing along the beach, knocked out tanks and landing craft until an AVRE's Petard silenced it in the afternoon. The 1st Hampshires lost their commanding officer and second-in-command on the beach.

civilopediaText.text: The cathedral town on the Caen-Cherbourg highway, home of the Bayeux Tapestry. The 50th Division entered it unopposed on the morning of June 7, making it the first town of any size to be liberated in France. It escaped the war almost undamaged, and on June 14 Charles de Gaulle made his first speech on French soil there.

civilopediaText.text: The harbour at the mouth of the Seulles, in the middle of Juno Beach. Offshore reefs delayed the landing until the rising tide had covered the beach obstacles, and the Royal Winnipeg Rifles and the Regina Rifles had to clear the strongpoints house by house. Juno cost the Canadians about 1,000 casualties, 359 of them killed.

The airfield on the plain west of Caen - the 3rd Canadian Division's final objective for D-Day. The North Nova Scotia Highlanders and the Sherbrooke Fusiliers were heading for it on June 7 when the 12th SS Panzer Division struck them at Authie and Buron. The Canadians finally took it on July 4.

civilopediaText.text: The capital of Lower Normandy, William the Conqueror's city, and the road and rail hub behind the British beaches - Montgomery's objective for D-Day. The 21st Panzer, 12th SS Panzer and Panzer Lehr Divisions all gathered round it, and the city was not taken until July, after it had been bombed into ruins.

Strongpoint WN 20, codenamed 'Cod', at La Brèche d'Hermanville in the middle of Sword Beach: bunkers, a 75mm gun, mortars and machine guns. The 1st South Lancashires and the 2nd East Yorkshires took it after a hard fight in the first hour, helped by the DD tanks and the AVREs.
KEY POSITION: in the D-Day scenario a city stands here at the start of the battle. At nightfall on June 8 the Allies win if they hold at least 10 of the 13 key positions; otherwise Germany wins.

The lifting bridge over the Caen Canal at Bénouville, and the bridge over the Orne at Ranville beside it. At 12:16 AM three Horsa gliders carrying Major John Howard's company of the Oxfordshire and Buckinghamshire Light Infantry landed within yards of the canal bridge, and both bridges were taken intact in ten minutes.
They held them until Lord Lovat's commandos arrived from Sword Beach at 1:30 PM, the bagpipes playing. The canal bridge was named after the 6th Airborne's emblem, the winged horse Pegasus.
KEY POSITION: in the D-Day scenario a city stands here at the start of the battle. At nightfall on June 8 the Allies win if they hold at least 10 of the 13 key positions; otherwise Germany wins.

Two tiny islands four miles off Utah Beach. At 4:30 AM 132 men of the 4th and 24th Cavalry Squadrons landed on them, thinking they held a German observation post - the first Allied troops to land from the sea on D-Day. The islands were empty, but mined.

name: Crisbecq Battery

civilopediaText.text: The Marcouf battery at Crisbecq: three Czech 210mm guns in huge casemates, the heaviest guns facing Utah. They sank the destroyer USS Corry and dueled with the battleship Nevada; the battery held out until June 12.

The bridge and causeway carrying the road from Sainte-Mère-Église across the flooded Merderet. For three days the 82nd Airborne fought for it against the 91st Division and its captured French tanks, until a bloody charge across the causeway on June 9 broke through.

name: Brecourt Manor
uniques: Blocks line-of-sight from tiles at same elevation

civilopediaText.text: The farm near Sainte-Marie-du-Mont where four German 105mm guns were firing on Utah Beach. On the morning of D-Day Lieutenant Richard Winters led about a dozen men of Easy Company, 506th Parachute Infantry, against them and destroyed the guns - a textbook assault still taught at West Point.

name: Vierville Draw
uniques: Has an elevation of [1] for visibility calculations

civilopediaText.text: Exit D-1 at Vierville, the western end of Omaha Beach - 'Dog Green', where Company A of the 116th Infantry lost nearly all its men in minutes. The draw was blocked by a concrete wall and guarded by WN 72 and WN 73.

name: Longues Battery
uniques: Has an elevation of [1] for visibility calculations

civilopediaText.text: Four 150mm naval guns in concrete casemates on the cliffs between Omaha and Gold, with a two-storey fire control post on the cliff edge. They dueled with HMS Ajax, HMS Argonaut and the French cruisers Georges Leygues and Montcalm until silenced; the garrison surrendered on June 7. The guns are still there today.

name: Douvres Radar Station
uniques: Blocks line-of-sight from tiles at same elevation

civilopediaText.text: A Luftwaffe radar station of concrete bunkers, minefields and wire inland from Juno Beach, garrisoned by some 230 men. Bypassed in the advance, it held out behind the Allied lines until June 17.

Four casemates on the coast east of the Orne, believed to hold guns that could fire on Sword Beach. Of the 600 men of Lt. Col. Terence Otway's 9th Parachute Battalion, only about 150 had gathered by 4:30 AM; they stormed the battery anyway, and found 75mm and 100mm guns. The Germans reoccupied it after the paratroopers left.
